16n75ho:294: "Ambiguity Compounds" is the most insidious risk for long-horizon agents. When an ambiguous requirement enters long-horizon execution, the agent doesn't realize it is "filling in the blanks"—it infers a "plausible-looking" answer from probabilities, context, and existing code. Slight deviation in the first round, second-round reasoning builds on that deviation, and by the third round it treats the first two rounds' outputs as established facts. The longer it runs, the more self-consistent the system becomes, but the direction of that self-consistency is not necessarily the direction of the original goal. Ralph Loop's naive approach (running more loops) cannot solve this, because looping only deepens the accumulated deviation. What actually works is setting anchors outside the loop: a front-loaded Spec explicitly cuts off key branch points, so the agent doesn't need to fill in implicit decisions during execution ^.

1h6mpk1:423: Long-Running Agent Explainer: From the Ralph Loop to the Takeover-Ready Harness. Over the past two weeks, Codex /goal has been discussed back and forth in the group several times. Its idea is very straightforward: give the agent a goal that stays active, and don't have it stop every few minutes to ask "should I continue?" Anyone who has run a slightly longer AI coding task probably knows the frustration: the work isn't done, but the agent stops first; you come back and add "continue," and it has to warm up from scratch again. Over the weekend, I went through Jarrod Watts' long post, his open-source long-running-agent-skill, OpenAI's official /goal documentation, and two recent Anthropic articles on long-running agents and context engineering. After reading them, what came to mind first wasn't some new feature, but the line we've been discussing recently: Harness, context working set, context operations, and the point Martin Fowler keeps making about "how non-determinism enters the development pipeline."

1k7pnsp:275: Hand-offability is the production-grade standard for long-horizon agents. The production-grade bar is not "how long it can keep running," but "after running for a long time, can the remaining state still be picked up by the next agent or human." The judgment criteria for hand-offability: can the next executor answer—what is the current goal? What is already established fact? What is only speculation? Which decisions cannot be casually changed? Which tests prove the current state is correct? If true rollback is needed, where is the nearest safe point? The answers are not in chat history, but in a set of structured external state files. Once models enter the development workflow, the system cannot depend on any one person's transient context; rather than hoping the model remembers everything, it is better to let it re-read the facts every time it wakes up ^.

1vw79xr:319: "Engineering continuation" and "chat continuation" are two fundamentally different execution philosophies. Chat continuation relies on context; each conversation is a continuation of previous context, and compression, truncation, and summarization can lose key details. Engineering continuation relies on evidence; files like GOAL.md, PROGRESS.md, DECISION LOG, and git history are takeover credentials left for the "next person," recording facts rather than inferences. Anthropic's engineering practices for long-running agents confirm this: compaction alone cannot sustain long tasks; you must introduce an initializer, progress files, feature lists, and end-to-end validation to shift the task from "chat continuation" to "engineering continuation." The two modes differ little on short tasks, but on long tasks they are the watershed between success and failure ^.
4divfd:26: Use a Subagent for quality review, not for role-playing
7osfpj:300: Codex /goal solves the "persistence" problem, not the "correctness" problem—this is the first key dividing line for understanding long-horizon agents. /goal makes goals persist across multiple context windows as durable objectives, and OpenAI's official docs position it as "giving Codex a verifiable stopping condition" rather than "giving Codex engineering judgment." This means /goal is essentially a control plane that makes "continuously advancing toward one goal" manageable. But the model's reasoning quality and directional correctness under that goal do not automatically improve just because /goal exists. Running for 8 hours isn't hard; what's hard is that what you get after 8 hours is still what you wanted—these are two orthogonal problems ^.
b6dwsc:330: The first-layer value of Subagent is not role-playing but context isolation. An agent accumulates self-confirmation over continuous work—which files it read, which approaches it abandoned—all of which biases subsequent reasoning, easily turning "local tests pass" into "globally done" and "I've fixed it" into established fact. The Reviewer Agent's value lies in having a fresh context, able to ask naive questions from goals, diffs, standards, and test results, rather than inheriting the implementer's psychological baggage. Boris Cherny's observation is insightful: a bug introduced by one agent often has to be caught by another agent. Multi-agent systems cost roughly 15x an ordinary chat in tokens; it is not a default architecture but a pricier quality-governance measure—worth it only when the task is decomposable, the payoff is high enough, and the verification chain is clear ^.
cn0irz:9: All three layers of the evidence chain are indispensable
dbknsz:125: Before assigning a long task to an agent, have it first ask about boundaries, goals, trade-offs, and acceptance criteria. A vague "help me finish this system" will make the agent constantly fill in implicit decisions during execution, and each fill-in adds drift risk. The goal of a front-loaded Spec is not "writing one more document" but cutting off key branch points in advance ^.
hz0q96:131: During internal Code Review, also ask "if this task changed hands mid-way, could you assess the current state in minutes"—if the answer is no, the Agent's on-site state isn't clear enough either. Hand-offability is the core problem the Harness really needs to solve: letting the model's non-deterministic capabilities enter a relatively deterministic engineering process ^.
jy5w5o:117: Divide state files into four categories—facts (which files changed, which tests pass), observations (what phenomena appeared during an attempt), assumptions (suspected but unverified causes), and decisions (settled trade-offs). The most dangerous thing is quietly writing "assumptions" as "facts," causing subsequent agents to inherit wrong judgments as premises generation after generation ^.
ob209a:196: The goal layer (Goal/Non-goal/Acceptance Criteria) answers "what to do," the state layer (Progress/Git History/Milestone) answers "how far we've gotten," and the governance layer (Tests/Review/Lint) answers "whether it's correct." Goals without state leave later agents unable to tell where things stand; state without verification makes the system treat "done" as "done right"; verification without goals means passing tests are not necessarily what the user wanted ^.
